blocks.text:
### How to use this guide

- **Who this is for.** A Java full stack developer preparing for interviews who needs a precise model of what the network does underneath REST calls, sockets, browsers and load balancers.
- **Every chapter follows the same steps:** (1) the concept and the problem it solves, (2) how it works, shown with diagrams of packets, message sequences and state machines, (3) a worked trace or calculation, (4) a hands-on experiment with real commands or Java code, (5) common failures, and (6) the questions interviewers ask, with answers.
- **How to study.** Read each diagram before the prose and try to narrate it aloud. Redo each worked trace on paper before reading the answer. Run the experiments; the output shown was produced on the machine that built this guide.
- **Running the code.** Save a Java listing as `Main.java` and run `java Main.java`. Commands marked as terminal sessions begin with `$`. Several tools (for example `tcpdump`, `dig` and `ping`) were not installed where the guide was built, so those outputs are shown as typical output and labelled.
- **Conventions.** Addresses use the documentation ranges (192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24) and private ranges, never real hosts. Numbers in a diagram match the accompanying trace.

A computer network is a set of devices that exchange data over shared communication infrastructure. Every REST call made by a Spring Boot service, every JDBC connection to a database and every page load in a browser is a sequence of messages crossing such infrastructure. The application code sees a `Socket` or an `HttpClient`; underneath, the data is cut into pieces, handed from device to device, and reassembled. A developer who understands this machinery can predict latency, explain timeouts and diagnose the failures that appear in production, which is the purpose of this guide.

This chapter defines the components of a network and the structure of the Internet, contrasts the two fundamental ways of moving data (circuit switching and packet switching), and contrasts the two common application architectures (client-server and peer-to-peer).

### Concept and mechanism

#### Components

The elements of a network are classified by function.

rows: Runs applications; originates and consumes data
Laptop, phone, web server, database server
Carries bits between two adjacent devices
Ethernet cable, optical fibre, Wi-Fi channel
Forwards frames within one local network using link-layer (MAC) addresses
Forwards packets between networks using network-layer (IP) addresses
Bridges wireless stations to a wired network
blocks.caption: Network components and their roles.

blocks.text:
A **host** is any device that runs application software at the edge of the network. Hosts are also called end systems. A **link** is a physical or wireless medium that joins two devices; its capacity in bits per second is its **bandwidth** or **rate**. A **switch** operates inside one local network and a **router** operates between networks; the difference is examined in the chapters on the link layer and on routing. A **packet** is a unit of data with a header that carries the information needed to deliver it.

#### Structure of the Internet

The Internet is a network of networks. Hosts connect to an **access network** (home broadband, a campus network, a mobile cellular network). Access networks connect to **Internet Service Providers** (ISPs). ISPs are arranged in tiers: regional ISPs buy transit from larger ISPs, and a small set of **tier-1 ISPs** reach every destination on the Internet without paying for transit, because they **peer** with each other. Content providers frequently operate their own global networks and connect directly to access ISPs. An **Internet Exchange Point** (IXP) is a facility containing a switching fabric at which many networks interconnect and exchange traffic locally.

blocks.text:
Each independently administered network is an **autonomous system** (AS) identified by a number. Autonomous systems exchange reachability information with the Border Gateway Protocol, described in the part on the network layer. Two consequences matter to developers. First, a request from a client to a server normally crosses several administrative domains, so no single party controls its latency. Second, the path is determined hop by hop by routers; the endpoints neither choose nor see it.

#### Packet switching and circuit switching

Two designs exist for moving data through a network core. In **circuit switching**, a dedicated path with reserved capacity is established between the endpoints before data flows and is released afterwards. The classic telephone network works this way. A link is divided by frequency (FDM) or by time slots (TDM), and each call owns one division for its whole duration, whether or not anything is being said.

In **packet switching**, the message is split into packets. Each packet carries the destination address and is forwarded independently by routers. Packets from many sources are interleaved on the same links; this sharing is called **statistical multiplexing**. A router uses **store-and-forward** operation: it receives a whole packet before it begins to transmit that packet on the outgoing link. If packets arrive faster than the outgoing link can send them, they wait in a buffer (a queue); if the buffer is full, packets are dropped.

blocks.caption: Circuit switching compared with packet switching.

blocks.text:
The Internet uses packet switching because computer traffic is bursty: a web page is fetched in a short burst and then the link is idle while the user reads. Reserving capacity for the idle periods would waste most of it.

#### Client-server and peer-to-peer

In a **client-server** architecture, a server host is always on, has a well-known address and answers requests from many clients; clients do not communicate with each other. Web servers, database servers and REST APIs follow this model. In a **peer-to-peer** (P2P) architecture, hosts act as client and server at the same time and exchange data directly. File-sharing systems such as BitTorrent use it, and so do some real-time communication paths (WebRTC). The advantage is that capacity grows with the number of peers. The costs are complexity, peers that appear and disappear, and difficulty of connecting hosts that sit behind NAT devices.

blocks.text:
### Worked trace

#### Why packet switching supports more users

Assume a 1 Mbit/s link. Each user, when active, transmits at 100 kbit/s, and a user is active 10 percent of the time. With circuit switching, each user reserves 100 kbit/s for the whole call, so the link supports 1000 / 100 = 10 users. With packet switching, 35 users may share the link. The link is overloaded only when more than 10 of the 35 users are active simultaneously. With independent users, the number of active users is binomially distributed, and the probability of exceeding 10 is the sum over k = 11 to 35 of C(35, k) \* 0.1^k \* 0.9^(35 - k).

blocks.title: Mux.java

blocks.code:
$ java Mux.java
circuit switching supports 10 users
packet switching with 35 users: P(more than 10 active) = 0.000424
640 kbit file, 64 kbit/s circuit, 0.5 s setup: 10.5 s
blocks.title: Run the calculation

blocks.text:
The result, 0.000424, means that the link is overloaded in about 0.04 percent of the time. Packet switching therefore carries 3.5 times as many users as circuit switching for almost the same quality, which is the quantitative reason for its dominance. The last line shows the other side of the trade: a circuit offers a fixed rate (64 kbit/s here), so the transfer time is predictable but cannot be shortened when the rest of the network is idle.

The interface `lo` is the loopback interface. Traffic sent to `127.0.0.1` never leaves the host, which is why all experiments in this guide that need a server use loopback. The interface `eth0` is a virtual Ethernet interface. The first octet of its MAC address, `02`, has the second-least-significant bit set, which marks a locally administered address (assigned by software rather than by the manufacturer).

A client-server exchange can be reproduced with the netcat utility `nc`, which opens plain TCP connections. One terminal acts as the server and a second as the client.

blocks.code:
$ nc -l 127.0.0.1 9000 > received.txt &
$ echo "hello over tcp" | nc -q1 127.0.0.1 9000
$ cat received.txt
hello over tcp
blocks.title: A one-shot TCP server and client on loopback

blocks.text:
The server host listens at a fixed address and port; the client initiates the connection. These two roles correspond exactly to `ServerSocket` and `Socket` in Java.

### Failure modes

- **Congestion loss.** A router buffer fills and packets are discarded. The symptom is retransmissions and slow transfers without any link being down. Diagnosis is by measuring loss and delay along the path (the tools chapter).
- **Path asymmetry and dependency on third parties.** The route to a server may cross networks the operator does not control. A fault in a transit network appears as high latency or timeouts from some clients only; the evidence is that the same request succeeds from another network.
- **Single points of failure at the edge.** A single access link or a single server is a client-server weakness: when it fails, every client fails. Remedies are redundancy (several servers behind a load balancer, several uplinks).
- **Assumption of a fixed path.** Packet switching does not guarantee in-order delivery or a fixed route; protocols above IP (TCP) must reorder and retransmit. Code that assumes one `read` returns one `write` is therefore incorrect.

### Questions to expect

1. What is the difference between a switch and a router? A switch forwards frames inside one local network using MAC addresses and a learned table. A router connects different networks and forwards packets using IP addresses and a routing table. A router also separates broadcast domains; a switch does not.
2. Why does the Internet use packet switching instead of circuit switching? Computer traffic is bursty. Statistical multiplexing lets many users share link capacity that circuits would reserve and leave idle. The cost is variable delay and possible loss.
3. What is store-and-forward? A router receives an entire packet before it starts to transmit it on the outgoing link. For a packet of L bits over N links of rate R, the end-to-end transmission time is at least N \* L / R.
4. What is an Internet Exchange Point? A facility with a switching fabric where many networks connect and exchange traffic directly. It shortens paths and lowers transit cost.
5. What is an autonomous system? A collection of IP networks under one administrative policy that is identified by an AS number and exchanges routes with other autonomous systems using BGP.
6. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of peer-to-peer over client-server. Advantage: capacity scales with the number of peers and no single server is a bottleneck. Disadvantage: peers are unreliable and frequently behind NAT, so connection setup and consistency are harder.
7. What does the loopback interface do? It delivers packets sent to `127.0.0.1` back to the same host without using any physical link. It is used for local testing and inter-process communication.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Follow-up chain: "Is the Internet a single network?" No. It is a network of tens of thousands of independently operated autonomous systems. Interconnection is by transit (a customer pays a provider) or by peering (two networks exchange traffic with each other), and routes are exchanged with BGP. No participant has a global view or control, which is why end-to-end latency and failures cannot be fully predicted from one side.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- A network consists of hosts at the edge, links, and switches and routers in the core; the Internet is a network of autonomous systems connected by transit and peering.
- Packet switching shares links by statistical multiplexing and uses store-and-forward; it is efficient for bursty traffic but introduces queueing delay and loss.
- Circuit switching reserves capacity per call: predictable but wasteful for bursty data.
- Client-server concentrates service on an always-on server; peer-to-peer distributes it among hosts.
- A packet does not follow a fixed path; applications must not assume ordering or message boundaries below TCP.

Network performance is described by three quantities: delay (how long a bit takes to arrive), loss (how many packets never arrive) and throughput (how many bits per second arrive). Application symptoms such as a slow API call or a stalled download are usually explained by one of them. This chapter defines the components of delay with their formulas, works through numeric examples, and introduces the bandwidth-delay product, which later explains TCP window sizes.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The four components of nodal delay

A packet travelling from one node to the next suffers four delays, whose sum is the **nodal delay**.

Microseconds or less; treated as constant
Waiting in the output buffer for earlier packets to be sent
Time to push all bits of the packet onto the link
L / R (L in bits, R in bit/s)
Time for a bit to travel across the medium
d / s (d distance, s propagation speed)

blocks.text:
Transmission delay and propagation delay are frequently confused. Transmission delay depends on the packet length and the link rate; it is the time to emit the packet, and it is not affected by distance. Propagation delay depends on distance and the medium; it is not affected by packet length or rate. The speed of a signal in copper or optical fibre is about 2 x 10^8 m/s, two thirds of the speed of light in vacuum.

#### Queueing delay and traffic intensity

Let a be the average packet arrival rate (packets per second), L the packet length in bits and R the link rate. The **traffic** **intensity** is La / R. If La / R is close to 0, packets rarely wait. As La / R approaches 1, the queue grows quickly; if La / R exceeds 1, the arrival rate is higher than the service rate, the queue grows without bound and packets are dropped when the buffer is full. The queueing delay is therefore the main source of variation in end-to-end delay, called **jitter** when measured as the variation between successive packets. Jitter is harmful to real-time media, which is why voice and video applications use playout buffers.

blocks.text:
#### Store-and-forward end-to-end delay

With N links in series, each of rate R, and no queueing, a single packet of L bits needs N \* L / R to reach the destination, because every router receives the whole packet before forwarding it. For P packets sent back to back, the last packet arrives after (N + P - 1) \* L / R, since the links work in a pipeline once it is filled.

blocks.text:
#### Loss

A packet is lost when a router buffer is full on arrival, when a link corrupts it so that a checksum fails, or when a device discards it (for example by a firewall rule or an expired TTL). Loss is a normal part of packet switching. Reliability is added above the network layer: TCP retransmits lost segments, while UDP leaves loss to the application.

#### Throughput and bottlenecks

**Throughput** is the rate at which bits are actually delivered between two hosts, as opposed to the **bandwidth**, which is the capacity of a link. For a path of links with rates R1, R2, ..., Rn, the maximum throughput of a single flow is min(R1, ..., Rn). The slowest link is the **bottleneck**. When several flows share a bottleneck of rate R, each obtains about R divided by the number of flows if the sharing is fair.

blocks.text:
#### Bandwidth-delay product

The **bandwidth-delay product** (BDP) is the number of bits that fit in the link between sender and receiver at one time: rate multiplied by delay. When the delay is the round-trip time (RTT), the BDP is the amount of data a sender must have sent and not yet had acknowledged in order to keep the link fully used. A sender that stops after each window until an acknowledgement arrives cannot exceed window / RTT. This is the basis of TCP window sizing; the transport part applies it.

blocks.text:
### Worked trace

#### Example 1: transmission and propagation delay

A packet of L = 1500 bytes = 12 000 bits is sent over a link of R = 10 Mbit/s and length 2000 km, with propagation speed 2 x 10^8 m/s.

1. d\_trans = L / R = 12 000 / 10 000 000 s = 0.0012 s = 1.2 ms.
2. d\_prop = 2 000 000 m / (2 x 10^8 m/s) = 0.010 s = 10 ms.
3. Time from first bit sent to last bit received = d\_trans + d\_prop = 11.2 ms. The first bit arrives after 10 ms; the last bit leaves the sender at 1.2 ms and arrives at 11.2 ms.
4. If R rises to 100 Mbit/s, d\_trans = 0.12 ms and the total is 10.12 ms; if R rises to 1 Gbit/s, d\_trans = 0.012 ms. The propagation delay does not change. Beyond some rate, a higher bandwidth no longer shortens the transfer of small messages, because propagation dominates.

#### Example 2: queueing

Let R = 10 Mbit/s and L = 12 000 bits, so one packet needs 1.2 ms. The service capacity is R / L = 833 packets per second. The traffic intensity for several arrival rates:

rows: Capacity reached; queue grows without bound
blocks.caption: Traffic intensity for L = 12 000 bits, R = 10 Mbit/s.

blocks.text:
#### Example 3: end-to-end with three links

Three links of 10 Mbit/s each, no queueing, one packet of 12 000 bits: 3 x 1.2 ms = 3.6 ms of transmission delay (diagram above). With ten such packets sent back to back, the last arrives after (3 + 10 - 1) x 1.2 ms = 14.4 ms.

#### Example 4: bandwidth-delay product

Rate 100 Mbit/s, RTT 40 ms. BDP = 100 x 10^6 x 0.040 = 4 x 10^6 bits = 500 000 bytes. A sender limited to a window of 65 535 bytes achieves at most 65 535 x 8 / 0.040 = 13.1 Mbit/s, which is 13 percent of the capacity.

#### Example 5: throughput of a file transfer

An 8 MB file (64 x 10^6 bits) is downloaded over a path whose bottleneck link is 2 Mbit/s. The transfer time is at least 64 x 10^6 / (2 x 10^6) = 32 s, independent of faster links elsewhere on the path.

### Hands-on

The calculations above are reproduced by a short program.

blocks.text: Delay observed by an application can be measured with `curl` and its `-w` format. The command below requests a local Java `HttpServer` (the server used throughout this guide, listening on 127.0.0.1:8080) and reports the connection time, the time to the first byte and the total time.

blocks.code:
$ curl -s -o /dev/null \
    -w 'connect=%{time_connect}s ttfb=%{time_starttransfer}s total=%{time_total}s\n' \
    http://127.0.0.1:8080/hello
connect=0.000104s ttfb=0.001190s total=0.001235s
blocks.title: Timing a request with curl (loopback; values vary between runs)

blocks.text:
On loopback the propagation delay is zero and the connect time reflects only local processing. Against a remote server, `time_connect` approximates one RTT (the three-way handshake needs one round trip before the client can send data), which makes it a convenient RTT estimate when `ping` is blocked. On a real path the output of `ping` and `traceroute` shows the per-hop and end-to-end delay; they are not installed on the build machine, so a typical ping output is shown in the tools chapter and is labelled as such.

### Failure modes

- **Bufferbloat.** Large buffers in routers or modems absorb bursts without dropping, so a saturated uplink adds hundreds of milliseconds of queueing delay. Symptom: ping time rises sharply while a large upload runs. Remedy: smart queue management (for example fq\_codel) or limiting the sending rate below the bottleneck rate.
- **Long fat networks.** A high-bandwidth path with large RTT (for example a transcontinental link) has a large BDP. Without a sufficiently large TCP window, throughput is far below the link rate although the link is idle. Diagnosis: throughput is approximately window / RTT.
- **Small-request latency dominated by round trips.** A client that issues many sequential requests pays one RTT per request. Moving from 20 sequential calls at 50 ms RTT (about 1 s) to one batched call (about 50 ms) is a design change, not a bandwidth upgrade.
- **Jitter in real-time traffic.** Variation of queueing delay breaks voice and video unless the playout buffer is dimensioned for it.
- **Loss misread as bandwidth shortage.** A path with 1 percent loss can show a small fraction of the link rate under TCP because the congestion window is reduced after each loss.

### Questions to expect

1. Name the four components of nodal delay. Processing, queueing, transmission and propagation delay. Only queueing delay varies significantly with load.
2. What is the difference between transmission delay and propagation delay? Transmission delay is L / R, the time to place the bits on the link; it depends on packet size and rate. Propagation delay is distance divided by signal speed; it depends on the medium and the distance only.
3. A 1500-byte packet crosses a 100 Mbit/s link. What is the transmission delay? 12 000 bits / 100 x 10^6 bit/s = 0.12 ms.
4. What is the bandwidth-delay product and why does it matter? It is rate multiplied by RTT, the amount of data in flight on a fully used path. A TCP window smaller than the BDP prevents the sender from filling the link.
5. What happens when traffic intensity approaches 1? The average queueing delay grows without bound and the buffer overflows; packets are lost.
6. What is the throughput of a path with links of 1 Gbit/s, 50 Mbit/s and 200 Mbit/s? 50 Mbit/s, the minimum, because the slowest link is the bottleneck.
7. Why does a faster link not always reduce latency? Higher rate reduces only transmission delay. Propagation, queueing and processing delay stay. For small messages over long distances, propagation delay dominates.
8. What is jitter? The variation in packet delay, mainly caused by variable queueing delay.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Nodal delay = processing + queueing + transmission + propagation; transmission is L / R and propagation is distance divided by signal speed.
- Queueing delay depends on traffic intensity La / R and rises sharply near 1; overflow produces loss.
- Store-and-forward makes the delay of N links at least N \* L / R for one packet.
- Throughput is limited by the bottleneck link; shared bottlenecks divide capacity among flows.
- The bandwidth-delay product is the data in flight needed to fill a path; windows smaller than the BDP waste capacity.

Moving a web page from a server to a browser involves electrical or optical signalling, error detection, addressing, routing, reliable delivery, encryption and the application protocol itself. A single monolithic design for all of this would be impossible to implement, test and evolve. Network architecture therefore divides the problem into **layers**. Each layer offers a service to the layer above, uses the service of the layer below, and hides how it is implemented. A layer can change (Wi-Fi replaces Ethernet, IPv6 replaces IPv4) without changing the layers above it. Two reference models describe the division: the OSI model and the TCP/IP model.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The OSI model and the TCP/IP model

The **OSI model** (Open Systems Interconnection, ISO standard) has seven layers. The **TCP/IP model** reflects the protocols actually deployed on the Internet and has four layers in its original form; textbooks commonly split its bottom layer in two and use five.

blocks.text:
In practice the three upper OSI layers are implemented by one application and its libraries, so the TCP/IP model merges them. The OSI numbers remain in everyday use: "layer 2 switch", "layer 3 router", "layer 4 load balancer" and "layer 7 proxy" refer to the OSI numbering. TLS has no clean place: it runs on top of TCP and below HTTP, and is placed at layer 5, 6 or "4.5" depending on the author. This is a property of the model, not an error.

#### Protocol data units

The unit of data handled by a layer is its **protocol data unit** (PDU). The names are conventional: a message at the application layer, a **segment** for TCP or a **datagram** for UDP at the transport layer, a **packet** (or IP datagram) at the network layer, a **frame** at the data-link layer, and bits at the physical layer. The terms "packet" and "datagram" are often used loosely; this guide uses the precise terms where the layer matters.

#### Encapsulation and decapsulation

When an application sends data, each layer treats the PDU received from above as opaque payload and prepends its own **header** (the data link layer also appends a trailer). This is **encapsulation**. The receiving host reverses the process: each layer reads and removes its header and passes the payload upward (**decapsulation**). A layer on one host communicates logically with the same layer on the other host (a peer-to-peer relation), but physically the data travels down the stack, across the medium and up the other stack.

blocks.text:
Intermediate devices implement only the lower layers. A switch processes layers 1 and 2; a router processes layers 1 to

1. Neither examines the TCP or HTTP content in normal operation. Only the end hosts implement all layers. A device

that works above its normal layer is a **middlebox**: a firewall that tracks TCP connections, a NAT device that rewrites ports, or a layer 7 proxy that parses HTTP.

blocks.text:
### Worked trace

#### An HTTP request from a host to a server in another network

Host A (192.168.1.10, MAC 02:42:ac:11:00:02) requests `/index.html` from `example.com`, assumed to resolve to the documentation address 203.0.113.80. The host and its default gateway (192.168.1.1, MAC 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e) are in one network; the server is in another. The TCP connection is already established; the client source port is 49152, the destination port is 80, the client sequence number is 1000 and the acknowledgement number is 5000. The steps below follow the first data segment.

1. **Application layer.** The HTTP client creates the 60-byte message `GET /index.html HTTP/1.1`, `Host:` `example.com`, `Accept: */*` and a blank line (each line ends with CR LF). It passes the bytes to the socket.
2. **Transport layer.** TCP adds a 20-byte header: source port 49152 (0xC000), destination port 80 (0x0050), sequence number 1000 (0x000003E8), acknowledgement number 5000 (0x00001388), header length 5 words (0x50), flags PSH and ACK (0x18), window 64240 (0xFAF0), checksum 0x1670 and urgent pointer 0. The segment is 80 bytes. The checksum covers the segment and a pseudo-header with both IP addresses.
3. **Network layer.** IPv4 adds a 20-byte header: version and header length 0x45, total length 100 (0x0064), identification 0x1C46, flags DF (0x4000), TTL 64 (0x40), protocol 6 for TCP, header checksum 0x204B, source address C0 A8 01 0A (192.168.1.10), destination address CB 00 71 50 (203.0.113.80). The packet is 100 bytes. The routing decision: 203.0.113.80 is not in the local network, so the next hop is the default gateway.
4. **Link layer.** The host needs the MAC address of the gateway (ARP, covered in the link layer chapter) and builds the Ethernet header: destination 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e, source 02:42:ac:11:00:02, type 0x0800. The data link layer appends the 4-byte frame check sequence (a CRC-32 over the frame, 0xC37F7484 here as computed by the program below). The frame has 118 bytes.
5. **Physical layer.** The network interface transmits the 118 bytes as signals, preceded by a preamble.
6. **At the router.** The router receives the frame, checks the FCS, removes the Ethernet header and reads the IP header. It selects the outgoing interface from the routing table, decrements the TTL from 64 to 63, recomputes the IP header checksum and builds a new Ethernet header with the MAC addresses of its outgoing link. The TCP segment and HTTP message are not modified.
7. **At the server.** The server's link layer accepts the frame (destination MAC is its own), IP verifies the header checksum and the destination address, delivers the segment to TCP because the protocol field is 6, TCP delivers the data to the process bound to port 80, and the HTTP server reads the 60 bytes.

blocks.caption: Header sizes and overhead for this request.

blocks.text:
The overhead is 58 bytes for 60 bytes of data. For large transfers the proportion falls: a full segment carries 1460 bytes of data in 1518 bytes on the wire (3.8 percent overhead), which is one reason bulk transfers use the largest segments the path allows.

### Hands-on

The program below builds the three headers of the trace byte by byte and computes the real checksums. It uses the Internet checksum of RFC 1071 (the same algorithm for IPv4 headers, TCP, UDP and ICMP) and `zlib.crc32` for the Ethernet frame check sequence.

blocks.code:
import socket
import struct
import zlib


def checksum(data):
    """Internet checksum (RFC 1071): ones-complement sum of 16-bit words, complemented."""
    if len(data) % 2:
        data += b"\0"
    total = sum(struct.unpack("!%dH" % (len(data) // 2), data))
    while total >> 16:
        total = (total & 0xFFFF) + (total >> 16)
    return ~total & 0xFFFF


http = b"GET /index.html HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: example.com\r\nAccept: */*\r\n\r\n"
src_ip, dst_ip = socket.inet_aton("192.168.1.10"), socket.inet_aton("203.0.113.80")

# TCP: ports 49152 -> 80, seq 1000, ack 5000, offset 5 words, flags PSH+ACK, window 64240
tcp = struct.pack("!HHIIBBHHH", 49152, 80, 1000, 5000, 5 << 4, 0x18, 64240, 0, 0) + http
pseudo = src_ip + dst_ip + struct.pack("!BBH", 0, 6, len(tcp))
tcp = tcp[:16] + struct.pack("!H", checksum(pseudo + tcp)) + tcp[18:]

# IPv4: version 4, IHL 5, total length, id 0x1c46, DF flag, TTL 64, protocol 6
ip = struct.pack("!BBHHHBBH4s4s", 0x45, 0, 20 + len(tcp), 0x1C46, 0x4000, 64, 6, 0, src_ip, dst_ip)
ip = ip[:10] + struct.pack("!H", checksum(ip)) + ip[12:]
# Ethernet: destination = gateway MAC, source = host MAC, type 0x0800 (IPv4)
eth = bytes.fromhex("001a2b3c4d5e") + bytes.fromhex("0242ac110002") + b"\x08\x00"
frame = eth + ip + tcp
fcs = zlib.crc32(frame)

print("HTTP payload :", len(http), "bytes")
print("TCP segment  :", len(tcp), "bytes (header 20)")
print("IPv4 packet  :", len(ip) + len(tcp), "bytes (header 20)")
print("Ethernet     :", len(frame), "bytes + 4 FCS =", len(frame) + 4)
print("Ethernet hdr :", eth.hex(" "))
print("IPv4 hdr     :", ip[:20].hex(" "))
print("TCP hdr      :", tcp[:20].hex(" "))
print("IP checksum  : 0x%04x   TCP checksum: 0x%04x   FCS: 0x%08x" % (
    struct.unpack("!H", ip[10:12])[0], struct.unpack("!H", tcp[16:18])[0], fcs))

blocks.text:
A Java program observes only the top of the stack: `socket.getOutputStream().write(bytes)` hands 60 bytes to TCP, and the operating system adds the TCP, IP and Ethernet headers. The application never sees the lower headers; they are visible only to a packet capture tool.

### Failure modes

- **Layer confusion in diagnosis.** A failure is easiest to locate by working through the layers in order: link up and ARP resolved (layers 1-2), IP reachable (layer 3), port open (layer 4), application responds correctly (layer 7). The troubleshooting part develops this into a playbook.
- **Headers reduce the usable payload.** A path MTU of 1500 bytes leaves 1460 bytes of TCP payload (1500 - 20 - 20). Additional encapsulation (a VPN or tunnel header, or a VLAN tag) reduces it further. If a sender uses a larger segment size than the path allows, packets are fragmented or dropped; the link layer chapter and the ICMP chapter explain path MTU discovery.
- **Violations of layering.** NAT rewrites addresses and ports (layers 3-4); stateful firewalls track TCP state; HTTP proxies terminate and reopen connections. These middleboxes are useful but they break the end-to-end principle: they can modify, delay or reject traffic that the endpoints consider correct, and they explain failures that no endpoint log records.
- **Checksum offload confusion.** A capture taken on the sending host may show incorrect TCP or IP checksums because the network interface computes them after the capture point. The packets are correct on the wire.
- **Assuming message boundaries.** TCP delivers a byte stream; one `write` of 60 bytes may arrive as several `read` results, and several writes may merge in one read. Protocols must define their own framing (HTTP uses Content-Length or chunked encoding).

### Questions to expect

1. Name the layers of the OSI model and the TCP/IP model. OSI: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application. TCP/IP: link (often split into physical and data link), internet, transport, application.
2. What is encapsulation? Each layer adds its own header (and for the link layer a trailer) around the PDU of the layer above. The receiver removes them in reverse order.
3. At which layer do switches, routers and load balancers operate? Switches at layer 2 (MAC addresses), routers at layer 3 (IP addresses), load balancers at layer 4 (IP and port) or layer 7 (HTTP content).
4. What are the PDUs of the transport, network and link layers? Segment (TCP) or datagram (UDP), packet, and frame respectively.
5. What is the purpose of layering? It separates concerns, lets each layer be replaced independently and allows interoperability through standard interfaces. The cost is some overhead and occasional violations for efficiency.
6. Which addresses change when a packet crosses a router, and which do not? MAC addresses change on every hop; IP source and destination addresses stay the same (unless NAT rewrites them). The TTL is decremented and the IP checksum recomputed.
7. Where does TLS belong in the layer models? It sits between the application protocol (HTTP) and TCP; it has no exact OSI layer and is commonly assigned to presentation or session.
8. A request carries 60 bytes of HTTP data. How many bytes are transmitted? With minimal TCP and IPv4 headers and an Ethernet frame: 60 + 20 + 20 + 14 + 4 = 118 bytes (excluding preamble and inter-frame gap).

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Follow-up chain: "Why do routers not look at TCP ports?" A router forwards by the destination IP address using its routing table and needs no transport information; this keeps forwarding fast and independent of the transport protocol. Devices that do examine ports (firewalls, NAT, layer 4 load balancers) are performing functions that go beyond forwarding. They must hold state per flow, which has a memory and failure cost.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Layers hide implementation and offer a service upward; the TCP/IP model has four or five layers, and the OSI numbers (2, 3, 4, 7) are used when naming devices.
- Each layer encapsulates the PDU from above: HTTP message, TCP segment, IP packet, Ethernet frame.
- For a 60-byte HTTP request the minimum overhead is 58 bytes (14 + 20 + 20 + 4); the figures can be reproduced by building the headers in code.
- MAC addresses are rewritten at every hop; IP addresses identify the endpoints and stay unchanged (apart from NAT).
- Switches work at layers 1-2, routers at 1-3, endpoints at all layers; middleboxes that go beyond their layer cause hard-to-diagnose behaviour.

The network layer delivers a packet between two hosts that may be many hops apart. The link layer solves a narrower problem: moving one packet across one link, from one node to an adjacent node. It defines how bits are grouped into **frames**, how nodes on a shared medium are identified (MAC addresses), how transmission errors are detected, and how devices that join several segments (switches) forward frames. Almost every host in a data centre or office uses Ethernet at this layer; wireless networks use Wi-Fi, described in the next chapter. The mechanisms in this chapter explain why a server on the same subnet answers faster than one reached through a router, how an IP address is converted into a hardware address, and why a misconfigured switch can bring down an entire floor.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Frames and MAC addresses

A **frame** is the PDU of the link layer: a header with addresses, the payload (an IP packet or an ARP message), and a trailer with an error-detection code. Every network interface has a **MAC address** (media access control address), a 48-bit number written as six hexadecimal octets, for example `02:42:ac:11:00:02`. The first three octets are the **organizationally unique identifier** (OUI) assigned to the manufacturer; the last three identify the interface. Two bits of the first octet have a defined meaning: the least significant bit marks a group (multicast) address, and the next bit marks a locally administered address, one assigned by software instead of by the manufacturer (virtual machines and containers use these). The address `ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff` is the **broadcast** address: every interface on the local network accepts the frame.

A MAC address is meaningful only inside one local network and has no topology information. An IP address identifies a host on the Internet and is assigned according to topology. A frame therefore carries the MAC address of the next hop, while the IP packet inside it carries the address of the final destination.

#### Ethernet frame format

blocks.text:
The fields are:

- **Preamble (7 bytes) and start frame delimiter (1 byte).** An alternating bit pattern that allows the receiver to synchronise its clock. These bytes are produced by the interface hardware and do not appear in captures.

#### • Destination and source MAC addresses (6 bytes each).

- **Type (2 bytes).** Identifies the payload protocol: 0x0800 for IPv4, 0x0806 for ARP, 0x86DD for IPv6, 0x8100 for an 802.1Q VLAN tag. Values of 1500 or less in this field are a length in the older IEEE 802.3 format.
- **Payload (46 to 1500 bytes).** A shorter payload is padded to 46 bytes so that the frame is at least 64 bytes. The upper limit of 1500 bytes is the **maximum transmission unit** (MTU).
- **Frame check sequence (4 bytes).** A CRC-32 computed over the header and payload. A receiver that finds a mismatch discards the frame silently; retransmission, if any, is the responsibility of a higher layer.

Between two frames the sender leaves an inter-frame gap of 12 byte times. The maximum frame is 1518 bytes (1522 with a VLAN tag).

#### Shared media, hubs and collisions

Early Ethernet used a shared coaxial cable and later a **hub**, a layer 1 repeater that copies every incoming bit to all other ports. All hosts then form one **collision domain**: if two transmit at once, the signals collide. Access was controlled by **CSMA/CD** (carrier sense multiple access with collision detection): a host listens before sending; if it detects a collision while sending, it stops, sends a jam signal and waits a random time chosen from a range that doubles after each successive collision (binary exponential backoff) before retrying. Hubs are obsolete. Modern Ethernet links are point-to-point and full duplex, so a host can send and receive at the same time and collisions do not occur.

#### Switches and MAC learning

A **switch** is a layer 2 device that forwards frames only to the port where the destination is located. It builds its **MAC** **address table** (also called the forwarding table or CAM table) automatically by **backward learning**:

1. When a frame arrives on a port, the switch records the source MAC address and the arrival port in the table, with a timestamp.
2. It looks up the destination MAC address. If the table has an entry for another port, the switch **forwards** the frame to that port only. If the entry points to the arrival port itself, the switch **filters** (discards) the frame, because the destination is on the same segment.
3. If the destination is unknown, or is a broadcast or multicast address, the switch **floods** the frame to all ports except the one on which it arrived.
4. Entries that are not refreshed expire; a common default is 300 seconds.

The switch is transparent: hosts do not know it exists and it needs no configuration to work.

blocks.text:
Because each port is its own collision domain and each link is full duplex, a switch gives every connected host the full link rate. A switch can forward in **store-and-forward** mode (the whole frame is received and its FCS checked before forwarding) or in **cut-through** mode (forwarding begins after the destination address has been read, lowering latency but forwarding corrupted frames).

#### Collision domains and broadcast domains

A **collision domain** is a set of interfaces whose frames can collide. A **broadcast domain** is a set of interfaces that receive each other's broadcast frames. A hub forms a single domain of both kinds. A switch gives each port its own collision domain but keeps all ports in one broadcast domain, because it floods broadcasts. A router does not forward link-layer broadcasts, so each router interface is a separate broadcast domain.

blocks.text:
Large broadcast domains are undesirable: every host must process every broadcast (ARP requests, DHCP discovery), and a switching loop turns one broadcast into a storm. Switches therefore run the **Spanning Tree Protocol** (STP, IEEE 802.1D and its faster variants), which blocks redundant links to leave a loop-free tree and unblocks them if an active link fails. Ethernet frames have no TTL, so a loop without STP circulates frames until the network is saturated.

#### VLANs and 802.1Q

A **virtual LAN** (VLAN) divides one physical switch infrastructure into several independent broadcast domains. A department or a service tier (web, application, database) can have its own VLAN without separate hardware. Each VLAN is identified by a 12-bit **VLAN ID**; the values 1 to 4094 are usable. Switch ports are of two kinds:

- An **access port** belongs to one VLAN. Frames on it are untagged; the switch adds the VLAN association internally.
- A **trunk port** carries several VLANs between switches (or to a router or server). Frames are marked with an **802.1Q** **tag** of 4 bytes inserted after the source MAC: a 16-bit TPID with the value 0x8100, then a 16-bit TCI containing a 3-bit priority (PCP), a 1-bit drop-eligible indicator (DEI) and the 12-bit VLAN ID. Frames of the **native VLAN** may be sent untagged on a trunk.

A frame never crosses from one VLAN to another at layer 2. Communication between VLANs needs a router (or a layer 3 switch), which has one interface or sub-interface per VLAN; each VLAN normally corresponds to one IP subnet.

blocks.text:
#### ARP: from IP address to MAC address

A host that wants to send an IP packet to a destination on the same subnet needs the destination MAC address. For a destination on another subnet it needs the MAC address of its **default gateway**. The **Address Resolution Protocol** (ARP, RFC 826) provides this mapping for IPv4. IPv6 uses the Neighbor Discovery Protocol for the same purpose.

The sender first consults its **ARP cache**. On a miss, it broadcasts an **ARP request** (Ethernet type 0x0806, destination ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff) asking "who has IP address X?". Every host on the segment receives it, but only the owner of X answers, with a unicast **ARP reply** that carries its MAC address. The requester stores the pair in its cache for a limited time (typically tens of seconds up to a few minutes, depending on the operating system) and sends the pending frame. A host also learns the sender's mapping from a received request, so one exchange usually populates both caches. A **gratuitous ARP** is a request or reply that a host sends for its own address, to announce a change or to detect an address conflict.

blocks.text:
ARP has no authentication: any host can send a reply, and the most recent one is accepted. This is the basis of ARP spoofing, covered in the part on security.

#### MTU and the link layer

The **MTU** is the largest payload, in bytes, that a link carries in one frame. For Ethernet it is 1500. The IP layer must not hand the link a packet larger than its MTU. TCP avoids the problem by limiting its segment to the **maximum segment** **size** (MSS): MTU - 20 (IPv4) - 20 (TCP) = 1460 bytes on Ethernet. Links differ: PPPoE (DSL) usually has 1492, tunnels subtract their encapsulation header (a VXLAN overlay adds 50 bytes), and data-centre networks sometimes use jumbo frames of about 9000 bytes. The smallest MTU along a path is the **path MTU**; discovery and fragmentation belong to the part on the network layer.

blocks.text:
### Worked trace

#### MAC learning on a four-port switch

Hosts A, B, C and D are attached to ports 1 to 4 of switch S1. Their MAC addresses are `aa:00:00:00:00:01` to `aa:00:00:00:00:04`; the table is initially empty. The following frames arrive, in order. The Java program in the next section computes the same result.

rows: Learn A on 1. B unknown: flood to ports 2, 3, 4. Table: A=1
Learn B on 2. A known on port 1: forward to port 1 only. Table: A=1, B=2
Learn C on 3. Broadcast: flood to ports 1, 2, 4. Table: A=1, B=2, C=3
A already known. C on port 3: forward to port 3 only
Destination unknown: flood to ports 2, 3, 4; no reply, no entry learned
blocks.caption: Table updates and forwarding decisions (frames 1 and 2 are the diagram above).

blocks.text:
Hosts D and the unknown address never appear in the table because D has not sent a frame; the switch learns only from source addresses. After 300 seconds without traffic, entries age out. If host B is moved from port 2 to port 4, the first frame it sends from the new port overwrites the entry (B=4) and traffic follows without configuration.

#### ARP resolution of the default gateway

Host A (192.168.1.10, MAC `02:42:ac:11:00:02`) sends to 203.0.113.80 via the gateway 192.168.1.1. Its cache has no entry for the gateway.

1. A builds an ARP request: operation 1, sender hardware address 02:42:ac:11:00:02, sender protocol address 192.168.1.10, target hardware address 00:00:00:00:00:00, target protocol address 192.168.1.1.
2. A wraps it in an Ethernet frame: destination ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, source 02:42:ac:11:00:02, type 0x0806. The 28-byte ARP message is padded to 46 bytes, so the frame is 64 bytes with the FCS.
3. The switch floods the frame to all ports of the VLAN. Hosts B and C compare the target address with their own, find no match and ignore the message.
4. The gateway recognises its address, records the sender's mapping (192.168.1.10 is at 02:42:ac:11:00:02) and sends a unicast reply: operation 2, sender hardware address 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e, sender protocol address 192.168.1.1, target hardware address 02:42:ac:11:00:02, target protocol address 192.168.1.10.
5. A stores 192.168.1.1 to 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e in its cache and transmits the original IP packet in a frame with destination MAC 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e.

Every later packet to an off-subnet destination reuses the cache entry. Note that A never obtains the MAC address of 203.0.113.80: ARP resolves only addresses on the local network.

### Hands-on

The simulator below implements the learning rules above with a `LinkedHashMap` as the MAC address table.

blocks.title: SwitchSim.java

blocks.text:
Frames 1 and 5 are flooded, frame 3 is a broadcast, and frames 2 and 4 are forwarded to a single port, as in the trace. A real switch adds a timestamp per entry, ageing, VLANs and a table of limited size.

ARP messages can be constructed explicitly. The following program builds the request and the reply of the trace and shows that each is 28 bytes, and that the frames are padded to the 64-byte Ethernet minimum.

blocks.code:
import socket
import struct

HOST_MAC = bytes.fromhex("0242ac110002")
GW_MAC = bytes.fromhex("001a2b3c4d5e")
HOST_IP = socket.inet_aton("192.168.1.10")
GW_IP = socket.inet_aton("192.168.1.1")


def arp(op, sha, spa, tha, tpa):
    # hardware type 1 (Ethernet), protocol 0x0800 (IPv4), HLEN 6, PLEN 4, operation
    return struct.pack("!HHBBH6s4s6s4s", 1, 0x0800, 6, 4, op, sha, spa, tha, tpa)


request = arp(1, HOST_MAC, HOST_IP, bytes(6), GW_IP)
reply = arp(2, GW_MAC, GW_IP, HOST_MAC, HOST_IP)
broadcast = bytes.fromhex("ffffffffffff")

# Ethernet type 0x0806 carries ARP; the payload is padded to the 46-byte minimum
frame1 = broadcast + HOST_MAC + b"\x08\x06" + request
frame2 = HOST_MAC + GW_MAC + b"\x08\x06" + reply
for name, pkt, frame in (("request", request, frame1), ("reply", reply, frame2)):
    padded = len(frame) + max(0, 60 - len(frame))
    print("ARP %-7s %d bytes: %s" % (name, len(pkt), pkt.hex()))
    print("  frame %d bytes before padding, %d padded, %d with FCS"
          % (len(frame), padded, padded + 4))

blocks.title: Typical output of ip neigh on a Linux host (typical, not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
`REACHABLE` means the entry was confirmed recently; `STALE` means it is still usable but will be re-verified on the next use; `FAILED` means that no reply was received, so the host is down or not on the segment. The flags value `0x2` in `/proc/net/arp` marks a complete entry. The interface MTU, which `Ifaces.java` from the first chapter printed (1400 on the build machine, 1500 on a typical Ethernet), can be changed with `ip link set dev eth0 mtu 1400` only for a value the whole path supports.

### Failure modes

- **Switching loop and broadcast storm.** Two switches connected by two cables without STP, or an accidentally patched cable, make frames circulate. Symptoms: all ports show full utilisation, LEDs blink in unison, hosts lose connectivity and CPU use of switches rises. Remedy: enable STP, enable storm control, remove the redundant link.
- **Duplicate IP address.** Two hosts claim one IP address, so the ARP cache of other hosts flips between two MAC addresses; connections to that address break intermittently. Diagnosis: `arp` or `ip neigh` shows the MAC address changing, and the ARP-based duplicate detection of the operating system logs a conflict.
- **ARP cache failures.** `FAILED` or `INCOMPLETE` entries mean that the target does not answer ARP: it is off, on another VLAN, or a firewall blocks ARP. The symptom is "destination host unreachable" from the local host, not from a router.
- **VLAN misconfiguration.** A port in the wrong VLAN, a missing VLAN on a trunk, or a native VLAN mismatch between two switches isolates a host or leaks traffic between segments. A host receives no DHCP offer or cannot reach its gateway although the link is up.
- **MTU mismatch and black holes.** A tunnel or VLAN tag lowers the usable MTU. Small packets (ping, TCP handshake) pass while large ones disappear, so a connection is established but stalls when data flows. The ICMP chapter covers diagnosis with the do-not-fragment flag.
- **MAC table exhaustion (CAM overflow).** An attacker or fault floods a switch with frames with random source addresses; the full table forces the switch to flood all traffic like a hub. Mitigation: port security limits per port.
- **Duplex mismatch.** One end fixed at half duplex while the other negotiates full duplex produces late collisions and poor throughput on an otherwise healthy link. Remedy: auto-negotiation on both ends.

### Questions to expect

1. What is a MAC address and how does it differ from an IP address? A 48-bit hardware address of an interface, meaningful on one local network and fixed by the manufacturer or software. An IP address is a logical address assigned by topology that identifies a host across networks. The MAC address changes at every hop; the IP addresses normally do not.
2. How does a switch learn? From the source address of every received frame, it stores the address and the arrival port. Frames for unknown or broadcast destinations are flooded; frames for known destinations are forwarded to one port.
3. What is the difference between a hub, a switch and a router? A hub repeats bits to all ports (layer 1). A switch forwards frames by MAC address (layer 2) and separates collision domains. A router forwards packets by IP address (layer 3) and separates broadcast domains.
4. What is the difference between a collision domain and a broadcast domain? A collision domain is the set of interfaces that can interfere with each other on a shared medium. A broadcast domain is the set that receives a link-layer broadcast. Switch ports are separate collision domains, but all ports of a VLAN share one broadcast domain.
5. What is a VLAN and why is it used? A logical partition of a switched network into separate broadcast domains, identified by a 12-bit ID. It limits broadcast traffic, isolates tiers or departments and avoids separate hardware. Inter-VLAN traffic needs a router.
6. Explain access and trunk ports. An access port carries one VLAN untagged. A trunk carries several VLANs between switches using 802.1Q tags (4 bytes, TPID 0x8100).
7. How does ARP work, and why is it a broadcast? The requester does not know the target MAC address, so it asks everybody on the segment; the owner of the IP address replies by unicast. Results are cached. ARP is limited to one subnet; for other destinations the host resolves the gateway.
8. What is the Ethernet MTU, and what is the MSS? The MTU is 1500 bytes of payload. The TCP MSS is MTU minus the IP and TCP headers, 1460 bytes.
9. Why does Ethernet need a minimum frame size? In the original half-duplex design a sender had to still be transmitting when a collision signal returned from the far end of the cable; a frame of at least 64 bytes guarantees it. The minimum is kept in full duplex for compatibility.
10. What stops a loop in a switched network? The Spanning Tree Protocol, which blocks redundant links, because Ethernet frames have no TTL.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Follow-up chain: "Host A pings host B on the same subnet for the first time. List every frame." First an ARP request (broadcast, A asks for B's MAC), then the unicast ARP reply from B. Then the ICMP echo request in a frame addressed to B's MAC, and the ICMP echo reply back. The switch learns A from the ARP request and B from the ARP reply, so the echo frames are forwarded to a single port. If A pings an address on another subnet, the ARP exchange is with the default gateway, not with the destination.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- The link layer moves frames across one link; MAC addresses identify interfaces locally and are replaced at every router hop.
- An Ethernet frame has a 14-byte header, 46 to 1500 bytes of payload and a 4-byte FCS; the MTU is 1500 and the TCP MSS 1460.
- A switch learns source addresses, forwards to a known port, and floods unknown and broadcast destinations; each port is a collision domain but all ports of a VLAN are one broadcast domain.
- VLANs create separate broadcast domains using 802.1Q tags (12-bit ID) on trunks; routing is required between VLANs.
- ARP resolves an IPv4 address on the local network to a MAC address using a broadcast request and a unicast reply, and has no authentication.

Wireless local networks, standardised as IEEE 802.11 and marketed as Wi-Fi, replace the cable of the link layer with a shared radio channel. The layers above (IP, TCP, HTTP) are unchanged, but the physical properties of radio alter the link layer design: the medium is shared by all stations within range, signals weaken and reflect, a station cannot listen while it transmits, and any device in range can receive the transmission. This chapter covers the structure of a Wi-Fi network, the association procedure, the access method CSMA/CA and why it differs from the CSMA/CD of classic Ethernet, the hidden terminal problem, and the radio bands. It is deliberately brief; developers meet these topics mostly as intermittent latency and packet loss on client devices.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Components and names

A **station** (STA) is any device with a Wi-Fi interface. An **access point** (AP) bridges the wireless stations to the wired network. An AP and its associated stations form a **basic service set** (BSS). Each BSS is identified by a **BSSID**, which is the MAC address of the radio of the AP. The human-readable network name is the **SSID** (service set identifier), up to 32 bytes. Several APs with the same SSID, connected by a wired network, form an **extended service set** (ESS); a station can move (**roam**) between APs of one ESS while keeping its IP address, because the APs and the wired network are one layer 2 network. One AP can broadcast several SSIDs, each with its own BSSID, often mapped to separate VLANs (for example staff and guests).

An 802.11 frame has up to four address fields, because a frame may be sent between a station, an AP and a wired destination. For a frame from a station to the AP, the receiver address is the BSSID, the transmitter address is the station, and the third address is the final destination on the wired network. Frames are classified as management (beacon, probe, authentication, association), control (RTS, CTS, ACK) and data frames.

#### Association

A station joins a network in three phases, shown below.

1. **Discovery.** The AP broadcasts a **beacon** frame about ten times per second with its SSID, supported rates and security capabilities. A station finds networks by listening (passive scanning) or by sending a **probe request** and receiving a probe response (active scanning).
2. **Authentication and association.** The station sends an authentication request and then an association request naming the SSID and its capabilities; the AP answers with a status and an association ID. In WPA3-Personal the authentication frames carry a password-based key exchange (SAE) instead of the empty "open system" exchange used by earlier modes.
3. **Key establishment.** In a protected network (WPA2 or WPA3) a four-message **4-way handshake** (carried in EAPOL frames) proves that both sides know the pairwise master key and derives the session keys that encrypt all data frames.

After the link layer association is complete, the station is an ordinary host on the layer 2 network and obtains an IP address with DHCP (described in the part on the network layer).

blocks.text:
#### CSMA/CA instead of CSMA/CD

Wired Ethernet detected collisions by listening while sending. A radio cannot do this: its own transmission is millions of times stronger than the signal it would need to detect, and a collision occurs at the receiver, which may be out of range of the other sender. 802.11 therefore uses **CSMA/CA** (collision avoidance) in a procedure called the distributed coordination function:

1. A station with data senses the channel. If it has been idle for a **DIFS** (distributed inter-frame space), it transmits immediately.
2. If the channel is busy, the station waits until it becomes idle, then waits one DIFS and counts down a random **backoff**, a number of time slots chosen from the **contention window**. The counter is frozen while the channel is busy and resumes when it is idle again. The station transmits when the counter reaches zero.
3. The receiver sends an **ACK** frame after a shorter gap, the **SIFS**, so that no other station can interrupt between data and ACK.
4. If no ACK arrives, the sender assumes a collision or a corrupted frame, doubles the contention window (from 15 slots up to a maximum of 1023) and retries, up to a retry limit; after the limit the frame is dropped.

blocks.text:
Unlike Ethernet, every unicast data frame is individually acknowledged at layer 2. This explains why Wi-Fi hides most radio loss from TCP, and why the cost is variable delay: a frame retried several times adds milliseconds of jitter without any packet being lost at the IP layer.

#### The hidden terminal problem and RTS/CTS

Two stations may both be in range of the AP but out of range of each other. Each senses an idle channel and transmits; the frames collide at the AP, and neither station can detect it. This is the **hidden terminal problem**. The remedy is optional: the sender first transmits a short **RTS** (request to send), the AP replies with a **CTS** (clear to send), and every station that hears either frame defers for the announced duration. The exchange costs overhead, so it is used only for large frames or in environments with hidden stations.

The opposite case, the **exposed terminal**, occurs when a station defers although its transmission would not interfere with an ongoing one; it reduces efficiency but causes no errors.

#### Bands, channels and standards

Wi-Fi operates in unlicensed spectrum. The **2.4 GHz band** offers longer range and better wall penetration but only three non-overlapping 20 MHz channels (1, 6 and 11 in most regions), and it is shared with Bluetooth, cordless phones and microwave ovens. The **5 GHz band** offers many more channels, wider channels and less interference but a shorter range. The 6 GHz band was added from Wi-Fi 6E onward for still more channels.

*IEEE 802.11 generations (maximum rates are theoretical aggregate PHY rates; real throughput is far lower).*

Higher rates depend on signal quality: a station far from the AP uses a more robust but slower modulation, and because all stations share airtime, one slow station reduces the throughput of the others (the "rate anomaly"). Application-visible throughput on Wi-Fi is typically half or less of the PHY rate, because of contention, acknowledgements and protocol overhead.

### Worked trace

#### Backoff after a busy channel

Contention window 0 to 15 (16 values), slot time 9 microseconds. Station A transmits. Station B has a frame ready while the channel is busy.

1. B senses the busy channel and defers; it draws a backoff of 3 slots but does not start counting.
2. A finishes its frame. The AP waits a SIFS and sends the ACK. The channel is busy until the ACK ends.
3. When the channel has been idle for one DIFS, B starts counting: after 3 idle slots (27 microseconds) its counter reaches zero and it transmits.
4. If a third station C had drawn the same value 3, both would transmit simultaneously. Neither receives an ACK; each doubles its window (0 to 31) and draws again.

The probability that two or more stations draw the same smallest value grows quickly with the number of stations, which is why dense Wi-Fi networks lose airtime to collisions. The simulation below draws a backoff from 0 to 15 for each of n stations and counts the rounds in which the smallest value is drawn by at least two stations.

### Hands-on

stations=20  P(collision at first attempt, CW=16) = 0.503
blocks.title: Run the simulation (fixed random seed 42; the values are reproducible)

blocks.text:
For 2 stations the result matches the analytical value 1/16 = 0.0625. With 20 stations about half of all contention rounds end in a collision at the first attempt, even though each station transmits rarely. This is the reason for contention window doubling, for limiting the number of stations per AP and for using several APs on different channels.

Reading the output: the BSSID is the AP identifier; `freq: 5180` means 5 GHz channel 36; the signal level in dBm is negative, and the closer to zero the stronger it is (about -50 dBm is excellent, -70 dBm is marginal, -80 dBm and below is unreliable); the bit rates are the currently negotiated PHY rates, which adapt continuously to the signal. A Java program cannot read these values through the standard library; on a laptop they are visible through operating system tools.

### Failure modes

- **Co-channel and adjacent-channel interference.** Many APs on the same or overlapping channels share airtime or corrupt each other's frames. Symptom: high latency and low throughput although the signal level is good. Diagnosis: scan for nearby networks and their channels; remedy: use 5 GHz and non-overlapping channels, lower transmit power.
- **Weak signal and rate fallback.** At low signal the PHY rate falls, so each frame occupies the channel longer; all stations on the AP slow down. Remedy: add or move APs, avoid obstacles.
- **Retries masked as latency.** The link layer retransmits a lost frame invisibly, so TCP sees no loss but sees delay jitter. Symptom: video calls stutter while `ping` shows occasional spikes of tens of milliseconds.
- **Roaming failures.** A station stays attached to a distant AP ("sticky client") until the signal is very poor, and a roam between APs on different VLANs changes the subnet and breaks connections. Remedy: roaming standards (802.11r/k/v), one VLAN per SSID across all APs.
- **Connected without connectivity.** Association succeeds, but DHCP fails, the DHCP pool is exhausted or a captive portal blocks traffic until the user signs in; HTTP requests are redirected to a login page. Applications see unexpected redirects or TLS errors.
- **Security misconfiguration.** Open networks and WEP or WPA(1) expose traffic; use WPA2 or WPA3, and never rely on the SSID being hidden.
- **Dense environments.** Hundreds of stations in one room overload the contention mechanism; the collision probability shown above is the mechanism.

### Questions to expect

1. What is the difference between SSID and BSSID? The SSID is the network name, which several APs may share. The BSSID is the MAC address of one AP radio and identifies one BSS.
2. Why does Wi-Fi use CSMA/CA and not CSMA/CD? A radio cannot detect collisions while transmitting, and collisions occur at the receiver. Wi-Fi therefore avoids collisions with random backoff and detects loss by a missing link layer ACK.
3. What is the hidden terminal problem and how is it solved? Two stations in range of the AP but not of each other cannot sense one another and collide at the AP. RTS/CTS lets the AP announce the reservation to both.
4. What are the steps for a station to join a WPA2 network? Discovery (beacon or probe), authentication, association, the 4-way handshake (keys), then DHCP for an IP address.
5. Compare 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz. 2.4 GHz has longer range and wall penetration but three non-overlapping channels and heavy interference. 5 GHz has more and wider channels and less interference but a shorter range.
6. Why is Wi-Fi throughput lower than the advertised rate? The advertised value is a theoretical PHY rate. Airtime is shared, every frame needs backoff and an ACK, headers add overhead, and signal quality lowers the rate in use.
7. Why can Wi-Fi make a TCP connection slow without packet loss? The link layer retransmits lost frames, so no loss reaches IP, but each retry adds delay and jitter, which TCP perceives as an increased and variable RTT.
8. What does roaming require? APs of one ESS connected by a layer 2 network so that the station keeps its IP address, plus fast re-association and key handling.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- A BSS is one AP and its stations (identified by the BSSID); an ESS is several APs with one SSID on one layer 2 network that permit roaming.
- Joining involves discovery, authentication, association and (for WPA2 and WPA3) a 4-way handshake before DHCP.
- CSMA/CA avoids collisions with sensing, random backoff with doubling contention windows, and per-frame ACKs; collisions grow quickly with the number of stations.
- Hidden terminals cause collisions that carrier sense cannot see; RTS/CTS reserves the channel.
- 2.4 GHz offers range and three non-overlapping channels; 5 GHz offers capacity and less interference; real throughput is far below the PHY rate.

A small set of command-line tools answers most questions about a network problem. Each tool observes one layer, so the choice of tool depends on the layer under suspicion. This chapter describes what each tool does and how to read its output. Commands for which the build machine has the tool (`curl`, `nc`, `openssl`) are run for real. The machine has no `ping`, `traceroute`, `ip`, `ss`, `tcpdump` or `dig`, and no access to the public Internet; for those tools the output is labelled **typical** and uses documentation addresses (192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24 and the RFC 1918 ranges) and the names `example.com` and `example.org`. Where the kernel exposes the same information in `/proc/net`, a real equivalent is shown, and a small packet-capture program written in Python reproduces the essential function of `tcpdump` on the loopback interface.
