blocks.caption: The standard tools.

blocks.text:
#### ping

`ping` sends ICMP echo requests and prints one line per echo reply. It measures reachability and the round-trip time at layer 3. It does not test any port or application.

blocks.code:
$ ping -c 4 example.com
PING example.com (203.0.113.80) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 203.0.113.80: icmp_seq=1 ttl=52 time=23.4 ms
64 bytes from 203.0.113.80: icmp_seq=2 ttl=52 time=22.9 ms
64 bytes from 203.0.113.80: icmp_seq=3 ttl=52 time=24.4 ms
64 bytes from 203.0.113.80: icmp_seq=4 ttl=52 time=23.7 ms

--- example.com ping statistics ---
4 packets transmitted, 4 received, 0% packet loss, time 3004ms
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 22.9/23.6/24.4/0.5 ms
blocks.title: Typical output of ping (typical, not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
Reading the output: `56(84) bytes` is the payload and the total IP packet size (56 + 8 bytes ICMP header + 20 bytes IP header). `icmp_seq` shows loss or reordering when numbers are missing. `ttl=52` is the remaining TTL of the reply; if the remote host started with 64, the reply crossed 12 routers. `time` is the RTT of each probe, and the last line summarises minimum, average, maximum and standard deviation (`mdev`, a measure of jitter). Many firewalls drop ICMP, so no reply does not prove that a host is down.

#### traceroute

`traceroute` discovers the routers on the path by sending probes with increasing TTL values (1, 2, 3, ...). A router that decrements the TTL to zero discards the packet and returns an ICMP "time exceeded" message that reveals its address; the destination returns a different answer, which ends the trace. Three probes are sent per TTL, so three times are printed.

blocks.code:
$ traceroute -n example.com
traceroute to example.com (203.0.113.80), 30 hops max, 60 byte packets
 1  192.168.1.1  1.1 ms  0.9 ms  1.0 ms
 2  198.51.100.1  8.2 ms  8.0 ms  8.4 ms
 3  * * *
 4  203.0.113.9  21.7 ms  21.5 ms  22.0 ms
 5  203.0.113.80  23.5 ms  23.2 ms  23.6 ms
blocks.title: Typical output of traceroute (typical, not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
A line with `* * *` means that no reply came: the router filters ICMP or rate-limits it; the path continues, as hop 4 shows. A large increase between two hops (hop 2 to 4 here) locates the link where delay is added, although a slow reply from one router alone may reflect only its slow handling of ICMP. Routes may differ for the forward and the return direction, and different probes may take different paths.

#### ip

`ip` (package iproute2) replaces the older `ifconfig`, `route` and `arp`. `ip addr` lists interfaces with MAC addresses, IP addresses and prefix lengths, `ip link` shows the link state and MTU, `ip route` shows the routing table and `ip neigh` shows the ARP cache.

blocks.code:
$ ip -brief addr
lo      UNKNOWN  127.0.0.1/8
eth0    UP       192.168.1.10/24
$ ip route
default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0 proto dhcp metric 100
192.168.1.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.1.10
blocks.title: Typical output of ip addr and ip route (typical, not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
The first route says that everything not matched by a more specific entry goes to the gateway 192.168.1.1; the second says that the local subnet is directly connected. The build machine reports the same structure in the raw kernel table, as the hands-on section shows.

#### ss

`ss` (socket statistics) lists sockets with their state, queue sizes and, with `-p`, the owning process. `ss -tln` shows listening TCP sockets, `ss -tan` all TCP sockets, and `ss -s` a summary.

blocks.code:
$ ss -tanp
State      Recv-Q Send-Q  Local Address:Port   Peer Address:Port  Process
LISTEN     0      100     0.0.0.0:8080         0.0.0.0:*          users:(("java",pid=2301,fd=45))
ESTAB      0      0       192.168.1.10:8080    192.168.1.50:51234 users:(("java",pid=2301,fd=61))
TIME-WAIT  0      0       192.168.1.10:8080    192.168.1.51:40022
blocks.title: Typical output of ss (typical, not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
For a listening socket, `Send-Q` is the configured backlog (the length of the accept queue) and `Recv-Q` the number of connections waiting in it; for an established socket they are bytes not yet read by the application and bytes not yet acknowledged by the peer. A growing `Recv-Q` on a connection means that the application is not reading fast enough. The state column is the main diagnostic: many `CLOSE-WAIT` sockets indicate that the application does not close connections, and many `TIME-WAIT` sockets are the normal result of closing many short connections. The transport part explains the states.

#### tcpdump

`tcpdump` captures packets on an interface and prints one line per packet. It needs administrator rights. A **capture filter** in Berkeley Packet Filter syntax limits the output (`tcp port 80`, `host 192.168.1.50`, `icmp`). Useful options are `-i` (interface), `-nn` (no name or port resolution), `-e` (show link-layer headers), `-w file.pcap` (write a file for Wireshark) and `-X` (hex and ASCII payload).

blocks.title: Typical output of tcpdump for the start of a connection (typical, not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
The flag `S` is SYN, `.` is ACK, `P` is PSH, `F` is FIN and `R` is RST. Each line shows the timestamp, the source address and port, the destination address and port, the flags, the sequence and acknowledgement numbers, the window and the payload length.

#### dig

`dig` queries DNS servers and shows the complete response. The answer section holds the records, the number after the name is the remaining time to live in seconds, and the footer shows which server answered and how long the query took.

blocks.code:
$ dig example.com A
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 41873
;; flags: qr rd ra; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 1, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 1

;; ANSWER SECTION:
example.com.    3600    IN    A    203.0.113.80

;; Query time: 18 msec
;; SERVER: 192.168.1.1#53(192.168.1.1) (UDP)
blocks.title: Typical output of dig (typical, not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
The status `NOERROR` with an answer means success; `NXDOMAIN` means that the name does not exist; `SERVFAIL` means that the resolver failed. The flag `ra` shows that the server offers recursion. The DNS chapter in the application layer part describes the protocol.

### Worked trace

#### Reading a packet capture

The program below is a minimal packet capture for the loopback interface. It opens a raw `AF_PACKET` socket, which is the facility that `tcpdump` uses, decodes the Ethernet, IPv4 and TCP headers and prints one line per packet with sequence numbers relative to the start of each direction (the same convention as `tcpdump` with default settings). Administrator rights are required. It needs the Python standard library only.

blocks.code:
import socket
import struct
import sys
import time

PORT = int(sys.argv[1])
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_PACKET, socket.SOCK_RAW, socket.htons(0x0003))
s.bind(("lo", 0))
s.settimeout(2)
base = {}
t0 = None
while True:
    try:
        frame, addr = s.recvfrom(65535)
    except socket.timeout:
        break
    # skip outgoing duplicates (packet type 4), non-IPv4 and non-TCP frames
    if addr[2] == 4 or frame[12:14] != b"\x08\x00" or frame[23] != 6:
        continue
    ihl = (frame[14] & 0x0F) * 4
    sp, dp, seq, ack, off, flags, win = struct.unpack("!HHIIBBH", frame[14 + ihl:30 + ihl])
if PORT not in (sp, dp):
    continue
plen = len(frame) - 14 - ihl - (off >> 4) * 4
t0 = t0 or time.time()
base.setdefault(sp, seq)
bits = ((2, "S"), (1, "F"), (4, "R"), (8, "P"), (0x10, "."))
names = "".join(n for b, n in bits if flags & b)
rel_ack = ack - base[dp] if dp in base and flags & 0x10 else 0
print("%6.3f ms  %5d > %-5d [%-2s] seq=%-4d ack=%-4d win=%-5d len=%d" % (
    (time.time() - t0) * 1000, sp, dp, names, seq - base[sp], rel_ack, win, plen))
blocks.title: sniff.py

blocks.text: While the sniffer is running, one request is made to the local server with `curl`; the output is the real capture of a complete HTTP exchange.

blocks.title: Capture of one HTTP request on the loopback interface (ports and timings vary between runs)

blocks.text:
Each line is interpreted as follows (the client port is 45390 in this run).

1. Lines 1-3, **three-way handshake.** The client sends a SYN with initial sequence number 0 (relative), the server answers SYN-ACK acknowledging 1, and the client sends the final ACK. The connection is established after 0.153 ms.
2. Line 4, **request.** The client sends 82 bytes with PSH and ACK. The 82 bytes are the HTTP request: `GET /hello` `HTTP/1.1` (21 bytes with CR LF), `Host` (22), `User-Agent` (24), `Accept` (13) and the empty line (2).
3. Line 5, **acknowledgement of the request.** The server acknowledges 83 (1 + 82): the acknowledgement number is the next byte expected.
4. Lines 6-9, **response.** The server sends 102 bytes (the status line and headers) and later 15 bytes (the body `Hello,` `network` and a newline), each acknowledged by the client: ack 103, then ack 118 (1 + 102 + 15). The Java `HttpServer` sends headers and body in two separate segments, which is visible here. The 2.0 ms gap before the response is the server processing the first request, including class initialisation.
5. Lines 10-12, **teardown.** The client sends FIN (sequence 83), the server acknowledges (ack 84) and sends its own FIN (sequence 118), and the client acknowledges that (ack 119). Each FIN consumes one sequence number.

The `win` values are the raw 16-bit window fields; after the window-scale option the effective window is larger (the SYN segments carry the unscaled value 65495 because the scale is not applied in a SYN). The capture shows 12 packets for one tiny request, and the data segments (82, 102 and 15 bytes) are a minority: protocol overhead dominates small exchanges.

### Hands-on

#### curl

`curl -v` prints the connection, the request and the response headers. `-I` sends a HEAD request, `-w` prints timing variables, `--max-time` limits the total time, `-k` accepts an untrusted certificate (testing only), and `--resolve` `host:port:address` forces an address without changing DNS.

blocks.code:
$ curl -sI http://127.0.0.1:8080/hello
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Date: Sat, 17 Oct 2026 16:48:35 GMT
Content-type: text/plain
blocks.title: Header-only request with curl -I

blocks.code:
$ curl -s --max-time 3 http://127.0.0.1:9999/
$ echo "exit status $?"
exit status 7
blocks.title: Exit status and error text for a connection that is refused

blocks.text:
Exit status 7 is "failed to connect"; status 28 would be a timeout. The difference between an immediate refusal (nobody listens on the port, or a firewall actively rejects) and a timeout (packets are dropped silently) is the most useful single fact in network diagnosis.

#### nc (netcat)

`nc -zv host port` tests whether a TCP port accepts connections without sending data. `nc -l` opens a listening socket, and `nc host port` is a raw TCP client.

blocks.code:
$ nc -zv 127.0.0.1 8080
Connection to 127.0.0.1 8080 port [tcp/http-alt] succeeded!
$ nc -zv 127.0.0.1 9999
nc: connect to 127.0.0.1 port 9999 (tcp) failed: Connection refused
blocks.title: Probing an open and a closed port

blocks.text:
#### openssl s_client

`openssl s_client` performs a TLS handshake and prints the negotiated parameters and the certificate. The following run connects to a local `openssl s_server` that uses a self-signed certificate created with `openssl req -x509 -newkey` `rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout k.pem -out c.pem -subj "/CN=localhost"`.

blocks.code:
$ echo | openssl s_client -brief -connect 127.0.0.1:8443
CONNECTION ESTABLISHED
Protocol version: TLSv1.3
Ciphersuite: TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
Peer certificate: CN = localhost
Hash used: SHA256
Signature type: RSA-PSS
Verification error: self-signed certificate
Server Temp Key: X25519, 253 bits
DONE
blocks.title: TLS handshake summary with s_client -brief

blocks.text:
The protocol version and the cipher suite are those negotiated; `Verification error: self-signed certificate` means that the chain does not lead to a trusted root, which is the cause of the `PKIX path building failed` exception in Java. The TLS part of this guide interprets all fields.

#### Sockets and routes from /proc

Without `ss` and `ip`, the kernel tables can be read directly. The program below decodes `/proc/net/tcp`, in which addresses are little-endian hexadecimal, and prints the rows that involve one port.

blocks.code:
import socket
import struct
import sys

STATES = {"01": "ESTAB", "02": "SYN-SENT", "06": "TIME-WAIT", "08": "CLOSE-WAIT", "0A": "LISTEN"}
port = int(sys.argv[1])


def addr(hexaddr):
    ip, p = hexaddr.split(":")
    dotted = socket.inet_ntoa(struct.pack("<I", int(ip, 16)))    # the kernel prints little-endian
    return dotted, int(p, 16)


print("%-10s %-22s %-22s" % ("State", "Local", "Peer"))
with open("/proc/net/tcp") as f:
    next(f)
    for line in f:
        parts = line.split()
local, peer = addr(parts[1]), addr(parts[2])
if port in (local[1], peer[1]):
    print("%-10s %-22s %-22s" % (STATES.get(parts[3], parts[3]),
                                 "%s:%d" % local, "%s:%d" % peer))
blocks.title: ss_lite.py
A listener and one established connection (an nc server and client on port 9102)

blocks.text: The listener, the client side and the server side of the connection appear as three sockets, which is what `ss -tan` would show. The routing table is available in `/proc/net/route`; the columns below are the interface, the destination, the gateway and the mask, each in little-endian hexadecimal.

blocks.title: The routing table of the build machine (real output, selected columns)

blocks.text:
Decoded, `010200C0` is the bytes C0 00 02 01 reversed, that is 192.0.2.1. The first row is the default route (destination 0.0.0.0, mask 0.0.0.0) through gateway 192.0.2.1; the second is the directly connected network 192.0.2.0 with mask 255.255.255.0 (`00FFFFFF` reversed is FF FF FF 00), the same two lines that `ip route` prints.

### Failure modes

- **Concluding from ping alone.** ICMP may be blocked while TCP works, or ICMP may pass while the application port is filtered. Test the actual protocol and port (`nc -zv`, `curl -v`).
- **Misreading traceroute.** Stars and high delay at one intermediate hop do not prove a fault if the following hops are fast: routers deprioritise ICMP generation. Load balancing can show different routers in one line. The path back may differ from the path out.
- **Capturing on the wrong interface or host.** Traffic that never reaches the interface of the capturing host is not visible; a capture on the client shows what the client sent, and a capture on the server shows what arrived. Comparing the two locates the loss.
- **Offload artefacts.** Segmentation and checksum offload make captures taken on the sending host show packets larger than the MTU or with wrong checksums. These are not faults.
- **Encrypted payload.** For HTTPS, `tcpdump` shows only the handshake and sizes; use the application's own logging or `curl -v` for content.
- **Blocking tools and DNS.** Without `-n`, `tcpdump`, `traceroute` and `ss` resolve names, which is slow and may itself generate DNS traffic that disturbs the analysis.
- **Permissions and containers.** Capturing needs root or the `CAP_NET_RAW` capability, and a container sees only its own network namespace.

### Questions to expect

1. How does traceroute work? It sends probes with TTL 1, 2, 3 and so on. Each router that reduces the TTL to zero returns an ICMP time-exceeded message that reveals its address; the destination answers differently and ends the trace.
2. What is the difference between "connection refused" and a timeout? Refused: a host answered with a TCP RST (or ICMP unreachable), so the host is up but no process listens or a rule rejects the connection. Timeout: no answer at all; packets are dropped by a firewall, the host is down or the route is broken.
3. A service is slow. Which tools are used first, and why? `curl -w` for the timing breakdown (connect, first byte, total), `ping` and `traceroute` for network delay and loss, `ss` for socket states and queues, and `tcpdump` when the evidence must be at packet level.
4. What does `Recv-Q` mean in `ss`? For an established connection, bytes received but not read by the application; for a listening socket, connections waiting in the accept queue.
5. How can an open port be tested without a browser? `nc -zv host port`, `curl -v telnet://host:port`, or in Java `new Socket().connect(address, timeoutMillis)`.
6. What does `ttl=52` in a ping reply tell? The remaining TTL of the reply packet; subtracting it from the likely initial value (64, 128 or 255) estimates the number of hops on the return path.
7. How is the certificate of a server inspected from the command line? `openssl s_client -connect host:443` `-servername host`, optionally piped into `openssl x509 -noout -text`, shows the chain, validity, subject and protocol.
8. Why can `tcpdump` show a checksum error for a correct packet? Checksum offload: the network card computes the checksum after the capture point, so the captured copy still holds a placeholder.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Follow-up chain: "An API call from a service to another fails intermittently. How is the diagnosis organised?" First reproduce with `curl -v` or a small client and note whether the failure is a refusal, a timeout or a reset, because each points to a different layer. Check name resolution (`dig`), reachability and loss (`ping`, `traceroute`), then the port and TLS (`nc -zv`, `openssl s_client`). On the server, check `ss` for listen-queue overflow, many `CLOSE-WAIT` sockets or `TIME-WAIT` build-up. If the evidence is still missing, capture with `tcpdump` on both ends and compare.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Select the tool by layer: curl and openssl (application), ss and nc (transport), ping and traceroute (network), ip neigh (link), tcpdump (all).
- ping measures RTT and loss with ICMP; traceroute uses increasing TTL; neither proves that a TCP service works.
- Refused, timed out and reset are three different symptoms with different causes.
- A capture shows the handshake, the byte counts of each segment and the sequence and acknowledgement numbers; a small program with an `AF_PACKET` socket reproduces the essence of `tcpdump`.
- The kernel tables in `/proc/net` hold the same information as `ss`, `ip route` and `arp`.
